options.optionText: A protocol providing full-duplex, bidirectional communication over a single persistent TCP connection.
options.explanation: Correct — unlike HTTP, WebSocket stays open so both sides can send messages independently at any time.

options.optionText: An HTTP method for pushing data from the server to the client.
options.explanation: There is no HTTP method for pushing — WebSocket is a separate protocol, not an HTTP method.

options.optionText: A browser API for storing data offline, similar to localStorage.
options.explanation: That describes Service Workers and IndexedDB — WebSocket is for real-time bidirectional network communication.

options.optionText: A REST API technique that uses long polling to simulate real-time updates.
options.explanation: Long polling uses repeated HTTP requests — WebSocket maintains a persistent connection without repeated requests.

options.optionText: WebSocket enables full-duplex real-time communication with low latency, avoiding the overhead of repeated HTTP request-response cycles.
options.explanation: Correct — HTTP requires a new request for each message; WebSocket keeps one connection open for instant bidirectional messaging.

options.optionText: WebSocket is more secure than HTTPS because it encrypts data at the application layer.
options.explanation: wss:// uses TLS like HTTPS — security is comparable; the advantage of WebSocket is real-time bidirectional communication.

options.optionText: WebSocket replaces REST APIs entirely and is better for all types of client-server communication.
options.explanation: WebSocket is best for real-time use cases — REST is simpler and more appropriate for request-response data fetching.

options.optionText: WebSocket eliminates the need for a backend server because browsers can communicate directly.
options.explanation: WebSocket still requires a server — it enables persistent client-server connections, not peer-to-peer without a server.

question: What is Short Polling and what are its problems?

options.optionText: The client sends HTTP requests at a fixed interval to check for updates — wasteful because most requests return no new data.
options.explanation: Correct — short polling works but burns bandwidth and server resources sending empty responses constantly.

options.optionText: A technique where the server sends data to the client at short intervals using a persistent connection.
options.explanation: That describes Server-Sent Events — short polling uses repeated client-initiated HTTP requests.

options.optionText: A WebSocket optimisation that sends smaller data frames to reduce latency.
options.explanation: Frame size is a WebSocket protocol detail — short polling is an HTTP-based technique, not WebSocket.

options.optionText: Short polling is always preferable to WebSocket because it works without special server support.
options.explanation: Short polling's bandwidth waste and latency make it a poor choice when WebSocket or SSE is available.

options.optionText: The client makes an HTTP request; the server holds it open until data is available, then responds — the client immediately re-requests.
options.explanation: Correct — long polling simulates push by holding requests open, reducing empty responses compared to short polling.

options.optionText: An HTTP technique where the client sends very large payloads to reduce request frequency.
options.explanation: Payload size is unrelated to polling strategy — long polling is about the server holding the connection until data is ready.

options.optionText: A WebSocket configuration option that increases the keep-alive timeout.
options.explanation: Long polling is an HTTP technique predating WebSocket — it is not a WebSocket configuration.

options.optionText: A browser feature that automatically retries failed HTTP requests after a delay.
options.explanation: Automatic retries are a different concern — long polling is a deliberate server-hold technique for near-real-time updates.

question: What different real-time communication techniques exist on the web?

options.optionText: Short polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events (SSE), WebSocket, and WebRTC — each with different trade-offs for latency, direction, and complexity.
options.explanation: Correct — choosing the right technique depends on whether you need bidirectional communication, browser compatibility, and infrastructure constraints.

options.optionText: Only WebSocket exists for real-time web communication — all other techniques are deprecated.
options.explanation: SSE, long polling, and WebRTC are all actively used — the best choice depends on the use case.

options.optionText: Real-time communication requires a native mobile app — browsers cannot do true real-time.
options.explanation: Browsers support WebSocket, SSE, and WebRTC natively for real-time communication.

options.optionText: HTTP/2 server push has replaced all other real-time techniques.
options.explanation: HTTP/2 server push is limited and largely deprecated in browsers — WebSocket and SSE remain the primary techniques.

options.optionText: A W3C standard for one-directional server-to-client streaming over HTTP, with automatic reconnection via the EventSource API.
options.explanation: Correct — SSE is simpler than WebSocket for pure server-push use cases like notifications and streaming AI responses.

options.optionText: A bidirectional protocol where both client and server can send messages at any time.
options.explanation: SSE is one-directional (server → client only) — bidirectional communication requires WebSocket.

options.optionText: A browser API for subscribing to server-side events using MQTT protocol.
options.explanation: SSE uses plain HTTP, not MQTT — EventSource is the browser API for consuming SSE streams.

options.optionText: An extension of WebSocket that reduces overhead by compressing frames.
options.explanation: SSE is a completely separate technique from WebSocket — it uses chunked HTTP transfer, not WebSocket frames.

question: What is the difference between WebSocket and Server-Sent Events?

options.optionText: WebSocket is full-duplex (both directions); SSE is server-to-client only. SSE uses plain HTTP; WebSocket uses a separate ws:// protocol.
options.explanation: Correct — SSE is simpler for push-only, WebSocket is needed for bidirectional real-time communication.

options.optionText: SSE requires a binary protocol; WebSocket uses plain text only.
options.explanation: This is backwards — WebSocket supports binary frames; SSE uses text over HTTP.

options.optionText: WebSocket is supported only in Chrome; SSE works in all browsers.
options.explanation: Both are widely supported in modern browsers — WebSocket has broader support if anything.

options.optionText: They are identical — the difference is only in naming convention between browser vendors.
options.explanation: They are fundamentally different protocols with different capabilities, connection models, and use cases.

question: What are the key features of Socket.io and how does it differ from raw WebSocket?

options.optionText: Socket.IO adds rooms, namespaces, automatic reconnection, and HTTP fallback on top of WebSocket — but a Socket.IO client cannot connect to a plain WebSocket server.
options.explanation: Correct — Socket.IO is a higher-level abstraction; its custom protocol is incompatible with raw WebSocket.

options.optionText: Socket.IO is a drop-in replacement for the browser WebSocket API with the same interface.
options.explanation: Socket.IO has its own protocol and API — it is not a drop-in for the native WebSocket object.

options.optionText: Socket.IO only works in Node.js environments and cannot be used in the browser.
options.explanation: Socket.IO has both a client (browser) library and a server (Node.js) library.

options.optionText: Socket.IO is slower than raw WebSocket and should only be used when IE11 support is required.
options.explanation: Socket.IO's overhead is minimal for most apps — its features (rooms, reconnection) justify its use beyond IE11 support.

question: WebSocket vs REST API for real-time data — which to choose?

options.optionText: WebSocket for continuous real-time streams (live prices, chat, collaboration); REST for request-response data fetching where real-time is not needed.
options.explanation: Correct — REST's simplicity wins for standard data fetching; WebSocket's persistent connection wins for high-frequency bidirectional updates.

options.optionText: Always use WebSocket — it is strictly better than REST in every scenario.
options.explanation: REST's simplicity, cachability, and browser tooling support make it better for most request-response use cases.

options.optionText: REST is always preferable because WebSocket connections are too complex to manage at scale.
options.explanation: WebSocket scales well with the right infrastructure — for live dashboards and chat, it is clearly the right choice.

options.optionText: The choice depends solely on message size — use WebSocket for large payloads, REST for small ones.
options.explanation: The key factor is communication pattern (bidirectional real-time vs request-response), not payload size.

question: When would you choose Server-Sent Events over WebSocket?

options.optionText: When communication is one-directional (server → client only) — e.g. live feeds, notifications, streaming AI responses — because SSE is simpler and traverses proxies easily.
options.explanation: Correct — SSE uses standard HTTP so it works without WebSocket-aware proxy configuration.

options.optionText: When you need bidirectional communication but want to save bandwidth.
options.explanation: SSE is one-directional — you cannot send messages from client to server over an SSE connection.

options.optionText: SSE is always preferable to WebSocket because it requires no handshake.
options.explanation: WebSocket's persistent connection is more efficient for high-frequency bidirectional messaging than SSE.

options.optionText: When you need to broadcast to millions of users — SSE scales better than WebSocket.
options.explanation: Scalability depends on infrastructure, not the protocol choice — both require horizontal scaling for large user counts.

question: How can WebSocket be better than Long Polling in terms of performance?

options.optionText: WebSocket eliminates repeated HTTP request/response overhead — one persistent connection handles all messages with much lower latency and bandwidth consumption.
options.explanation: Correct — long polling re-establishes HTTP connections for every message; WebSocket reuses one TCP connection.

options.optionText: WebSocket compresses data automatically; long polling sends data uncompressed.
options.explanation: Both can use compression — the performance advantage is connection reuse, not built-in compression.

options.optionText: Long polling is faster because it uses fewer server resources than maintaining persistent connections.
options.explanation: Long polling holds connections open too — WebSocket's efficiency comes from not re-establishing the connection per message.

options.optionText: WebSocket performance is identical to long polling — the choice is purely stylistic.
options.explanation: WebSocket has measurably lower latency and bandwidth usage for high-frequency messaging compared to long polling.

question: When would you use WebRTC over WebSocket?

options.optionText: For peer-to-peer audio/video streaming and low-latency data channels directly between browsers — WebRTC avoids routing media through a central server.
options.explanation: Correct — WebRTC is designed for real-time media; WebSocket routes everything through a server.

options.optionText: When you need a more secure connection than WebSocket provides.
options.explanation: Both wss:// and WebRTC use TLS — security is not the differentiator.

options.optionText: WebRTC should replace WebSocket for all chat applications because it is lower latency.
options.explanation: WebRTC adds NAT traversal complexity unsuitable for simple text chat — WebSocket is simpler and appropriate for most chat.

options.optionText: WebRTC is only for mobile applications — WebSocket is used on the web.
options.explanation: WebRTC runs natively in all modern browsers — it is a web standard, not a mobile-only technology.

question: How do you load balance WebSocket connections?

options.optionText: Use sticky sessions (session affinity) so all messages from a client hit the same server, plus a pub/sub layer (Redis) to broadcast messages across servers.
options.explanation: Correct — stateful WebSocket connections require sticky sessions; Redis pub/sub ensures messages reach all subscribed clients across nodes.

options.optionText: Round-robin load balancing works identically for WebSocket as for HTTP — no special handling needed.
options.explanation: Round-robin can break WebSocket connections mid-session — sticky sessions are required because the connection is stateful.

options.optionText: WebSocket cannot be load balanced — you must use a single server for all WebSocket traffic.
options.explanation: WebSocket can be load balanced with sticky sessions and a shared pub/sub layer like Redis.

options.optionText: Load balancing WebSocket requires switching to a binary protocol — JSON messages cannot be load balanced.
options.explanation: Message format is irrelevant to load balancing — the challenge is connection statefulness, not data encoding.

question: How would you secure WebSocket communication?

options.optionText: Use wss:// (TLS), authenticate on connection establishment (JWT in first message or cookie), validate all incoming messages, and apply rate limiting.
options.explanation: Correct — wss:// encrypts the channel; auth at connect time prevents unauthorised connections.

options.optionText: WebSocket is inherently secure — no additional security measures are needed.
options.explanation: ws:// sends data in plaintext — always use wss://, and authentication is essential to prevent unauthorised access.

options.optionText: Use API keys in the WebSocket URL query string for authentication.
options.explanation: Query strings appear in server logs — use cookies or an initial authenticated message to pass credentials.

options.optionText: Security is the browser's responsibility — server-side code does not need to validate WebSocket messages.
options.explanation: Never trust client input — validate and sanitise all messages server-side regardless of the transport protocol.

question: Would WebSocket be able to handle 1,000,000 concurrent connections?

options.optionText: Yes, with a distributed architecture: horizontal scaling, sticky load balancers, Redis pub/sub for cross-node messaging, and connection-efficient async server runtimes.
options.explanation: Correct — systems like Slack and Discord handle millions of connections by distributing across many nodes.

options.optionText: No — WebSocket is limited to ~1000 connections per server by the TCP stack.
options.explanation: Modern async servers can handle tens of thousands of connections per instance — 1M is achievable with horizontal scaling.

options.optionText: Yes, a single Node.js server can handle 1M WebSocket connections without any special configuration.
options.explanation: A single server has memory and file descriptor limits — 1M requires horizontal scaling across multiple nodes.

options.optionText: WebSocket connections are too resource-intensive — use SSE instead for large numbers of clients.
options.explanation: SSE also holds persistent connections — the scalability challenge is the same; the solution is horizontal scaling.

question: Explain how the WebSocket protocol works under the hood.

options.optionText: It starts with an HTTP/1.1 Upgrade handshake; once accepted (101 Switching Protocols), the TCP connection carries lightweight frames instead of HTTP messages.
options.explanation: Correct — the handshake reuses HTTP for initial negotiation, then the connection is 'upgraded' to the WebSocket framing protocol.

options.optionText: WebSocket opens a new UDP connection per message for low-latency delivery.
options.explanation: WebSocket uses TCP, not UDP — reliability is provided by TCP; WebRTC uses UDP for media streams.

options.optionText: WebSocket wraps every message in an HTTP request with a Connection: keep-alive header.
options.explanation: After the initial upgrade, WebSocket messages are not HTTP — they are binary frames on the raw TCP connection.

options.optionText: WebSocket uses a polling mechanism internally but abstracts it behind an event-based API.
options.explanation: WebSocket is a genuine persistent connection — it does not poll internally.

question: What is a WebSocket frame and what is the purpose of frame masking?

options.optionText: A frame is the basic data unit in WebSocket. Client-to-server frames must be masked (XOR with a random key) to prevent cache poisoning by intermediary proxies.
options.explanation: Correct — masking prevents intermediary infrastructure (proxies) from being confused by raw byte patterns that resemble HTTP.

options.optionText: Masking encrypts the WebSocket payload to provide confidentiality — it replaces TLS.
options.explanation: Masking is not encryption and provides no confidentiality — TLS (wss://) is required for encryption.

options.optionText: Frames are only used for binary data — text messages in WebSocket do not use the framing protocol.
options.explanation: All WebSocket messages, both text and binary, are sent as frames — the frame header includes a type bit distinguishing them.

options.optionText: Frame masking is optional and is typically disabled in production for performance.
options.explanation: The WebSocket spec mandates masking for client-to-server frames — it is not optional.

question: What is the fundamental difference between WebSocket and raw TCP? Why does WebSocket exist?

options.optionText: WebSocket runs over TCP but adds a message-framing layer and an HTTP-compatible handshake, allowing it to traverse existing web infrastructure (proxies, firewalls, load balancers).
options.explanation: Correct — raw TCP has no message boundaries or HTTP upgrade path; WebSocket solves both problems for browser environments.

options.optionText: WebSocket is faster than raw TCP because it compresses all payloads by default.
options.explanation: WebSocket does not compress by default — performance relative to raw TCP depends on framing overhead, not compression.

options.optionText: WebSocket replaces TCP with a more reliable transport layer protocol.
options.explanation: WebSocket runs on top of TCP — it does not replace TCP's reliability mechanism.

options.optionText: The only difference is that WebSocket uses port 80/443 while raw TCP uses port 8080.
options.explanation: Port choice is incidental — the key differences are framing, the HTTP handshake, and browser accessibility.
